caption:
The top band is narrowing. Where ten in a hundred once got an outstanding rating, many organisations are now forcing that down to seven. Three people who would have been excellent last year will be told they were good.

Understand what that does to the decision. With a flat 9.1% average increment projected for 2026, there is no money to soften the call. When output quality is comparable across the shortlist, the deciding question becomes who the room can already picture in the senior role.

That is a presence problem, not a performance problem. Nobody will tell you that in the feedback form.

And the call is not made in April. It is being shaped right now, in mid-year calibration meetings, by people describing you in two sentences to someone who has met you twice.

Bearing. Tone. Calculated silence. These are the things that decide how those two sentences read. In command, we trained them. In a boardroom, you can too.
alt_text: A plain dark slide with bold text reading: Ten percent were excellent. Now seven percent are. Below it, smaller text: the deciding factor is no longer your output. The Lumina Presence wordmark sits at the bottom.

topic.title: The bell curve is sharpening: only 7% can be excellent
topic.angle: When top ratings drop from 10% to 7% of employees, the deciding factor stops being output quality and becomes who decision-makers can picture in the senior role — which is a presence problem, not a performance problem.
topic.why_now: Indian organisations are in the Q3/H2 mid-year calibration and ratings-forecasting window, meaning the decisions that produce April's rating are being shaped right now, against Deloitte's and Aon's flat 9.1% increment headline.

rationale: A stark, text-only visual matches the no-nonsense tone and lets the narrowing-ratings statistic land without decoration.
